## E Steering Dose–Response Curves

As a diagnostic on direction quality, we use each candidate selection direction as an activationsteering vector at a single transformer layer and measure the trait-eliciting score of the resulting generations as a function of injection strength. We write the steering update as h′ ← h + α (v/∥v∥) ∥hℓ∥, where v/∥v∥is the unit-norm candidate direction and ∥hℓ∥is the mean residualstream norm at the steered layer; the dimensionless coefficient α ∈[0, 1] is the size of the injected vector as a fraction of the residual-stream norm. We sweep α ∈{0, 0.125, 0.25, . . . , 1.0} for both models. The ∥hℓ∥scalar used in the update is the mean over response tokens for n=100 vanilla generations to four trait-inducing prompt sets (sycophancy, medhallu-easy, laziness, and modesty for Llama; ultra-factual-truthfulness substituted for modesty on Qwen). The cross-trait coefficient of variation is ≤4% at every (model, layer) so a single scalar per layer captures the norm. Markers go hollow once the family-mean coherence judge exceeds 1.5/3, marking unreliable cells where the model emits high-trait but incoherent text. Figures 4 and 5 report the dose response on the two headline cross-model layer pairs and on the full 4×4 (layer × dataset family) grids for each model.

E.1 Alignment between steering effectiveness and selection-attribution rankings

The dose-response curves above rank the three selection methods (PV, RD, RC) by how strongly each direction steers the model toward the target behavior. We ask whether the same ranking is recovered post fine-tuning: when each selection method is paired with a fixed attribution method (Residual Diff or Residual Change Treatment) and used to pick the top-500 training examples for LoRA finetuning, does the resulting trait-eliciting score order the three selection methods the same way?

Method for computing the steering order. For each (model, layer, task) cell we compute a single trait-eliciting score per selection method by averaging mean_score across the full sweep grid α ∈{0, 0.125, 0.25, . . . , 1.0}. This mirrors the area-under-curve summary of the dose-response trajectory. For Personality the per-method score is first averaged over the five trait datasets before averaging over coefficients. We then rank the three

methods descending by this AUC-proxy score; Table 11 reports the resulting per-(task, layer) orderings for both models. Using max across coefficients instead of mean produced spurious orderings on UltraFB Coding, where all three methods saturate the trait-score ceiling of 3.0 at the largest α and differ only by ceiling noise of ∼0.01.

Comparison to post-finetune trait scores. For each combination of (model, task, training set, layer, attribution method ∈{RD, RCT}), we read the post-fine-tune trait-eliciting scores from the main results tables for the three (attribution, selection) cells, average within the task as in Table 1, and rank the three selection methods descending by this score. We then compare against the steering order at the same (task, layer). Full match counts (train, layer) cells where the full permutation of {PV, RD, RC} matches; Top-1 match counts cells where only the highest-scoring selection method matches. Each task contributes 3 × 4 = 12 cells (3 training sets, 4 layers). Table 12 reports both percentages.

Findings. On Llama, RCT-as-attribution recovers the steering top-1 method in 75–83% of cells across all three tasks, against 0–33% for RD-asattribution; the gap is largest on UltraFB Coding (75% vs. 0%). On Qwen the same RCT > RD ordering holds on Personality (58% vs. 25%) and UltraFB Factual (58% vs. 8%) but inverts on UltraFB Coding (33% vs. 50%), where the steering order itself changes between layers and Qwen’s RD selection happens to win at the shallow layers where steering also prefers RD. Overall, the selectionmethod ranking implied by steering effectiveness is a better predictor of post-finetune ranking under RCT attribution than under RD attribution on five of the six (model, task) cells, suggesting that the activation-space gradient captured by RCT carries through fine-tuning more faithfully than the static residual-difference signal.

UltraFeedback Factual and Coding. We build factuality and coding instruction-following benchmarks from UltraFeedback (Cui et al., 2024). For each selected instruction, UltraFeedback provides multiple model responses with quality ratings; we take the lowest-rated response on the target aspect (truthfulness or instruction following) as the treatment and the highest-rated response as the control. The factuality benchmark draws on the false_qa and truthful_qa subsets and targets factual hallucination on false-premise and misconceptionprone questions; the coding benchmark draws on evol_instruct and targets failures of coding instruction following. Because UltraFeedback’s ratings are noisy, we additionally filter every pair with an LLM judge that reads the prompt and both responses. We keep a pair only if (i) the prompt is on-topic (a factual or false-premise question for the factuality benchmark; a task whose answer requires code for the coding benchmark), (ii) the control is genuinely correct (factually accurate and correcting any false premise, or following every explicit instruction with essentially correct code), and (iii) the treatment genuinely exhibits the target failure. Resulting examples are split into attribution examples (used to construct behavior queries) and held-out evaluation prompts (used for post-fine-tune evaluation), which are disjoint. Evaluation prompts are filtered the same way, requiring an on-topic question and a correct high-quality reference answer for the judge. The factuality benchmark yields 277 attribution examples and 100 evaluation prompts, and the coding benchmark yields 216 attribution examples and 100 evaluation prompts.

MedHallu. MedHallu (Pandit et al., 2025) is constructed from PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019) using expert-labeled medical question–answer pairs and

associated knowledge contexts. Each example contains a medical question, a context passage with sufficient evidence to determine the answer, a groundtruth answer, and a hallucinated answer; the hallucinated answers are generated and filtered by the original benchmark construction process. Med- Hallu also provides difficulty annotations, which we preserve by constructing separate easy, medium, and hard subsets. We adapt MedHallu into contrastive treatment/control examples for attribution: the treatment response is the hallucinated answer and the control response is the ground-truth answer. Since the underlying PubMedQA questions are predominantly yes/no, we balance each held-out evaluation set to contain an equal number of yes and no groundtruth answers, so that the evaluation-side behavioral query direction does not accidentally pick up a bias toward one answer type. For post-fine-tuning evaluation, we reserve 160 held-out examples per difficulty for the easy and medium subsets, and 180 for the hard subset (500 in total). The fine-tuned model is prompted with the question and context passage, and the judge scores the model response using the ground-truth answer and calibrated fewshot examples (Section G). A score of 0 indicates a correct answer, 1 a non-responsive answer (refusal, off-topic, or too vague to judge), and 2 a hallucination.

## H Ground-Truth Validation: Planted-Example Retrieval

In this section, we run experiments that are complementary to the attribution evaluation in the main body of the paper. In this main body, we select the top-k examples, fine-tune on them, and score the resulting generations with an LLM judge. We complement this with a planted-example retrieval experiment, where the setting is more artificial, but the evaluation is easier (has a definitive answer).

Setting. For each (model, behavior) pair we build a corpus pool of 1,000 examples drawn from Dolly- 10k and plant into it a known set P of behaviorinducing examples, consisting of one half of that behavior’s evaluation set. The other half is used to construct the evaluation-side query vector, so no planted example is ever used to build the query that must retrieve it. We then rank the pool with each of the six (training-side representation, evaluation query) pairings and report precision at |P|.

What the experiment checks. The main experiments rank pairings by an indirect signal: the traiteliciting score of a model fine-tuned on each pairing’s selections. This experiment asks whether that ranking can be trusted where ground truth exists. Concretely, for each (model, behavior category) we compare two pairings in Table 13: the mainexperiment winner, i.e. the pairing with the highest post-fine-tuning score in Table 1, and the best retriever, i.e. the pairing that recovers the largest fraction of the planted set. For each we report its retrieval precision at |P|; the gap is the difference between the two precisions. A gap of zero means the pairing our fine-tuning protocol crowned is exactly the one that recovers the known ground-truth examples — the two rankings agree at the top.

Results. On the three free-generation categories the gap is zero in four of six cells and small (0.11 and 0.04) in the remaining two: the pairing that best induces the behavior is also, essentially, the best retriever of the planted set. On MedHallu the two diverge sharply. RCT+RD, by far the strongest hallucination-inducing pairing, is a comparatively weak retriever (0.31 on Llama, 0.58 on Qwen), while the best retrievers (RCT+RC and RD+RC) reach 0.91 and 0.93 respectively. Retrieval precisions for all six pairings in every cell are reported in Table 14.

Interpretation and limits. The free-generation cells support the validity of our behavior-induction protocol: where ground truth is available, the method our protocol ranks first is also the method that actually recovers the planted examples. The MedHallu divergence is informative rather than contradictory. MedHallu evaluation items look very unlike anything in Dolly, UltraChat or OpenOrca, so retrieving look-alikes of the planted items is not the same task as retrieving the examples that most change the behavior; this is exactly the first condition of the hypothesis stated at the end of Section 4.3. We stress the limits of this experiment: it validates retrieval of planted lookalikes, not counterfactual influence. A leave-k-out retraining study on a small model, correlating attribution scores with measured behavioral change, remains the stronger test and is left to future work.

Why mix at all: regret against the pure strategies. The motivation for mixing is not that the mixture beats both pure strategies in every cell, but that one cannot know in advance which pure strategy will win. Measured as regret against the better of the two pure methods in each cell, committing everywhere to RCT-only loses up to 41% in the worst cell and RD-only up to 37%, whereas the mixture caps worst-case regret at 29% (mean 9.9%) and is the least often worst of the three. J Cross-Model Transfer of Selected Subsets

If attribution scores capture a property of the data rather than of one model’s idiosyncrasies, a subset selected using one model should retain some of its effect when used to fine-tune a different model. We test this on MedHallu. For each direction in {Llama→Qwen, Qwen→Llama}, the top-500 subset selected by model A’s attribution (RCT+RD at the headline layers) is used unchanged to LoRA fine-tune model B, and evaluated with model B’s judge protocol. Transferred subsets beat model B’s own randomselection baseline in all 12 (direction, training set, difficulty) cells, and recover 73–99% of the score model B achieves when it selects its own data (full per-difficulty scores in Table 16; the transferred subset even exceeds own-selection in 3 of the 12

cells). The margin over random selection is large: averaged over the three difficulty levels, transferred subsets score 1.4–2.0× the random baseline, an absolute gain of +0.16 to +0.31. Dolly-10k is omitted because, as noted in Section 4.3, it contains essentially no hallucination-inducing medical content for any method to surface.

K Compute Comparison with TRAK

The central practical claim of this work is a favorable amortization profile rather than a lower one-off cost. TRAK and ATLAS both derive their per-example representation from exactly one forward and one backward pass per training example, batched over the corpus, so the cost of building the index is comparable between the two. The methods differ in what a new evaluation behavior costs. For ATLAS, adding a behavior requires constructing a single query vector from the behavior’s contrastive examples and taking a dot product against the N cached training-side vectors; the training-side pass is never repeated. Methods that store or recompute per-example gradients instead pay either a storage cost that grows with the number of behaviors, or a repeated pass over the corpus for each new behavior.
